lessons.name: Analytic vs numerical IK shoot-out
lessons.summary: Compare equation-based and iterative inverse kinematics on the same five-joint arm, measuring failures as carefully as speed.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Compare equation-based and iterative inverse kinematics on the same five-joint arm, measuring failures as carefully as speed.

![SO-101 follower arm, a possible five-joint positioning chain for the benchmark](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-ik.webp)
*SO-101 follower arm, a possible five-joint positioning chain for the benchmark. Source: [Published setup](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/so101), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **Inverse kinematics (IK)** turns a desired gripper position and orientation into joint angles; **forward kinematics (FK)** computes the pose from those angles.
- **Analytic IK** solves geometry directly; **numerical IK** repeatedly improves an initial guess. Think of comparing two implementations behind the same API, with identical test fixtures.
- **A degree of freedom** is an independent motion coordinate: five arm joints cannot independently satisfy all six position-and-orientation coordinates.

> **Key idea:** A solver comparison is meaningful only when every method solves the same constrained task.

## What you need

- **Laptop simulation:** Use a laptop, one documented five-joint model, Robotics Toolbox for Python, TRAC-IK, and a geometric solution derived for that particular chain.
- **Starting point:** Finish Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim and read Inverse kinematics (analytic & numerical); no physical arm purchase is required.
- **Shared contract:** Specify which orientation components matter, joint limits, pose tolerance, initial guesses, and timeout before collecting results.

## Steps

1. **Validate FK:** Display known joint configurations and confirm the gripper frame and joint order.
2. **Generate reachable targets:** Sample valid joint angles, then compute their poses with FK; save the inputs so every solver receives identical targets.
3. **Implement the adapters:** Return angles, success, elapsed time, and residual, meaning the remaining target error; distinguish unsupported tasks from failed solves.
4. **Run the comparison:** Include repeated seeds, unreachable positions, and targets near joint limits; retain timeout cases.
5. **Check returned angles:** Recompute FK independently and reject limit violations rather than trusting a success flag.
6. **Demo the results:** Replay selected successes and failures beside a table of success rates and solve times.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  J[Valid angles] --> F[FK targets]
  F --> S[Three solvers]
  S --> V[FK and limit checks]
  V --> T[Benchmark table]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **False fairness:** The Toolbox's general analytic interface targets six-axis arms; do not silently substitute that model for your five-joint derivation.
- **Fast failures:** An immediate rejection is not a fast successful solve; report successful timings and timeout behavior separately.

## When it's done

- **Worked sanity check:** Feed a target generated from a saved configuration back into each solver; different returned angles are acceptable if FK reaches the same permitted pose.
- **Reproducible artifact:** Publish model revision, target set, task constraints, and raw results, including an empty target-set case that produces no misleading averages.

```python
if sol.success:
    verified_pose = robot.fkine(sol.q)
    print(sol.residual)
```

lessons.name: Build a 3D-printed delta picker
lessons.summary: Build a printed parallel robot that transfers small objects, then measure positioning error and completed picks per minute.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Build a printed parallel robot that transfers small objects, then measure positioning error and completed picks per minute.

![Printed delta robot with three branches meeting at a moving platform](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-delta.webp)
*Printed delta robot with three branches meeting at a moving platform. Source: [Published setup](https://github.com/grzesiek2201/Delta-Robot), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **A delta robot** joins a fixed platform to a moving platform through three branches; paired passive rods keep the moving platform parallel to the base.
- **Parallel kinematics** means those branches cooperate on one tool position. Unlike separate software workers, they cannot choose mutually inconsistent endpoints.
- **Measured performance** separates commanded coordinates from actual placement, and attempted picks from objects successfully delivered to a tray.

> **Key idea:** Mechanical alignment and calibration matter as much as correct inverse-kinematics code.

## What you need

- **Choose one complete design:** The pictured DIY Delta robot provides models, a parts list, build instructions, and offline visualization; do not mix its dimensions with another build.
- **Hardware access:** Arrange printing, the selected motors and controller, joints, power supply, and a lightweight pickup tool; your local parts cost is unknown.
- **Preparation:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim and study Parallel & closed-chain mechanisms before powering the assembled robot.
- **Published comparison:** Low-cost 3D-printed delta robot (IJMERR 2024) uses three servos, Arduino Uno, and a PCA9685 servo driver; its measurements are not guarantees.

## Steps

1. **Simulate the geometry:** Enter the chosen design's dimensions and test safe reachable points before ordering or printing parts.
2. **Assemble and inspect:** Check branch lengths, free joint movement, and a secure fixed platform; document deviations from the design.
3. **Calibrate the motors:** Establish consistent zero angles and verify each branch independently with small motions.
4. **Add the pickup sequence:** Approach, collect, lift, transfer, and release; treat a missed pickup as a failed cycle.
5. **Measure repeated placements:** Use fixed test locations, record commanded and observed positions, and separate accuracy from repeatability.
6. **Demo the picker:** Transfer small wrapped sweets or similarly lightweight objects while logging completed cycles and elapsed time.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Pick location] --> K[IK angles]
  K --> M[Move branches]
  M --> G[Pick and place]
  G --> E[Measure outcomes]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Overclaiming speed:** The IJMERR paper reports 30 picks per minute and 2.2 mm positioning accuracy on its apparatus, not on every printed delta.
- **Mechanical hazard:** Keep fingers clear of moving rods and disconnect motor power before adjusting joints.

## When it's done

- **Worked calculation:** Convert successful transfers divided by elapsed seconds into picks per minute by multiplying by 60; count drops separately.
- **Honest result:** Show repeat trials, failed pickups, placement error, and an unreachable-command rejection, not only the fastest successful video.

```python
picks_per_minute = 60 * successful_transfers / elapsed_seconds
```

lessons.name: CAD-to-sim pipeline for a custom gripper
lessons.summary: Design a gripper assembly in Onshape, export it into MuJoCo, and demonstrate a repeatable simulated cube grasp.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Design a gripper assembly in Onshape, export it into MuJoCo, and demonstrate a repeatable simulated cube grasp.

![Menagerie's Robotiq gripper and hanging cube, a reference setup rather than the proposed custom design](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-gripper.webp)
*Menagerie's Robotiq gripper and hanging cube, a reference setup rather than the proposed custom design. Source: [Published setup](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie/tree/main/robotiq_2f85), BSD-2-Clause.*

## What you will learn

- **Computer-aided design (CAD)** describes parts and their assembly; a simulator also needs joints, masses, contact geometry, and actuators, which apply forces or motion commands.
- **The export pipeline** resembles a compiler: the assembly is source code, named mates are declarations, and the exported robot description is a build artifact.
- **A collision shape** is the geometry used for contact calculations; a pretty visual mesh alone does not establish a working grasp.

> **Key idea:** Successful export proves the file can be read, not that its mechanics or contacts are correct.

## What you need

- **Software and access:** Use Onshape, authorized API access, onshape-to-robot, and MuJoCo; simulation requires no printed hardware, while account eligibility and local costs need checking.
- **Preparation:** Revisit Intro: CAD and 3D-print a robot part and Robot description formats (URDF / MJCF).
- **A modest design:** Start with a fixed palm and simple moving fingers; use the pictured Robotiq scene as a contact reference, not as your original CAD.

## Steps

1. **Create the assembly:** Separate rigid links and constrain their intended motion; put the fixed base first in the top-level assembly.
2. **Name the mates:** Use the exporter conventions, including dof_ for movable joints and frame_ for a useful fingertip frame.
3. **Export to MuJoCo:** Set output_format to mujoco in config.json, then inspect the generated robot.xml and scene.xml.
4. **Audit the model:** Check mass, joint axes, travel limits, collisions, and actuator behavior before adding a cube.
5. **Tune the grasp:** Place a cube between open fingers, close slowly, and test whether it stays held during a prescribed movement.
6. **Demo a clean rebuild:** Re-export the same assembly and replay the test with documented initial conditions and failure counts.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Onshape assembly] --> X[Export configuration]
  X --> M[MuJoCo model]
  M --> V[Joint and contact checks]
  V --> G[Cube grasp]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Missing declarations:** Unrecognized mates do not become controllable joints; orphaned links can become fixed to the base.
- **Artificial success:** Interpenetrating fingers or excessive contact friction can hide bad geometry; inspect contacts rather than judging only the animation.

## When it's done

- **Worked export check:** A slider named dof_finger becomes a prismatic, or straight-line, joint; a frame_tip becomes a MuJoCo site for inspection.
- **Reproducible delivery:** Save assembly revision, export settings, simulator model, and grasp trials, including a cube placed outside the opening.

```json
{
  "url": "YOUR_ONSHAPE_ASSEMBLY_URL",
  "output_format": "mujoco"
}
```

lessons.name: Camera-to-gripper frame chain on the SO-101
lessons.summary: Project the SO-101 gripper's computed coordinate frame onto a camera image and measure how well the overlay matches reality.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Project the SO-101 gripper's computed coordinate frame onto a camera image and measure how well the overlay matches reality.

![SO-101 follower whose gripper frame will be projected into a camera view](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-frames.webp)
*SO-101 follower whose gripper frame will be projected into a camera view. Source: [Published setup](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/so101), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **A coordinate frame** is an origin plus three directions; the same physical gripper point has different coordinates in the robot base and camera frames.
- **A rigid transform** combines rotation and translation in a 4-by-4 matrix. Chaining transforms is like composing typed functions: adjacent input and output frames must match.
- **Camera intrinsics** describe image formation, including focal lengths and image center; **extrinsics** describe where the camera sits relative to the robot.

> **Key idea:** An overlay tests the entire geometry chain, not just whether an individual matrix looks plausible.

## What you need

- **Starting setup:** Complete Assemble & teleoperate an SO-101, then begin with a simulated arm and camera before testing a fixed real camera.
- **Software:** Use FK, meaning joint angles converted into a gripper pose, plus OpenCV calibration and projection; existing-hardware cost depends on your lab.
- **Map foundations:** Read Rigid-body motion & coordinate frames and Forward kinematics (DH & product of exponentials); record your joint order and units.

## Steps

1. **Define the frames:** Label base, gripper, and camera; write down which direction every stored transform maps.
2. **Calibrate the camera:** Collect a checkerboard from varied views, retaining the image resolution, camera matrix, and lens-distortion coefficients.
3. **Locate the camera:** Estimate its pose relative to a known target attached at a measured pose relative to the robot base.
4. **Compute the chain:** Combine camera-from-base with base-from-gripper FK to express the gripper origin and axis endpoints in camera coordinates.
5. **Project the axes:** Draw those endpoints into the image with the calibrated camera model; compare visible reference points across multiple arm poses.
6. **Demo and measure:** Display the live overlay with per-pose pixel errors and keep the camera fixed during the evaluation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  J[Joint angles] --> F[Base to gripper FK]
  F --> C[Camera coordinates]
  C --> P[Camera projection]
  P --> O[Overlay and error]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Wrong direction:** OpenCV's solvePnP maps object coordinates into camera coordinates; invert it when your chain requires the opposite direction.
- **Convention mismatch:** OpenCV's camera axes point right, down, and forward; robot model axes need not use that convention.
- **Timing mismatch:** Compare camera frames with corresponding joint readings; moving an arm while pairing unrelated samples can spoil an otherwise correct chain.

## When it's done

- **Worked chain:** Camera-from-base multiplied by base-from-gripper yields camera-from-gripper; reversing the multiplication is not equivalent.
- **Measurable evidence:** Save images, calibration, and pixel-error statistics, including points behind the camera and missing-image handling; hardware stays stationary while checking an uncertain overlay.

```python
T_camera_gripper = T_camera_base @ T_base_gripper
point_camera = T_camera_gripper @ point_gripper
```

lessons.name: Centroidal momentum viewer
lessons.summary: Animate a simulated humanoid with its center of mass and whole-body momentum displayed beside the motion.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Animate a simulated humanoid with its center of mass and whole-body momentum displayed beside the motion.

![Unitree H1 model in MuJoCo Menagerie, a possible humanoid for the viewer](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-momentum.webp)
*Unitree H1 model in MuJoCo Menagerie, a possible humanoid for the viewer. Source: [Published setup](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie/tree/main/unitree_h1), BSD-3-Clause.*

## What you will learn

- **Center of mass (CoM)** is the mass-weighted average of all body positions; it moves when the robot changes posture, even if the feet remain still.
- **Linear momentum** measures translational motion weighted by mass; **angular momentum** measures rotational motion about a specified point, here the whole-body CoM.
- **Centroidal** means expressed about that center. The viewer is like a debugger showing aggregate state beside the individual objects that produced it.

> **Key idea:** Whole-body momentum compresses many joint motions into a useful summary, but does not certify balance.

## What you need

- **Simulation assets:** Choose a humanoid such as Menagerie's H1, plus Pinocchio and a 3D viewer; no physical humanoid purchase is needed.
- **Consistent model data:** Use matching geometry, masses, joint order, and base conventions for rendering and dynamics; do not silently mix unrelated robot descriptions.
- **Preparation:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim, then read Floating-base & centroidal dynamics (legged/humanoid).
- **A floating base** is a torso that can translate and rotate instead of being bolted down; include its position and velocity in the state.

## Steps

1. **Load the model:** Display a neutral pose and inspect the total mass and body locations before calculating any overlays.
2. **Supply a motion:** Replay a documented trajectory with positions and velocities, or generate a clearly labeled kinematic animation rather than claiming a balanced controller.
3. **Compute the quantities:** Use Pinocchio's centerOfMass and computeCentroidalMomentum interfaces with the same current state.
4. **Draw separate overlays:** Add a CoM marker and labeled linear and angular momentum vectors, each with its own units and visual scale.
5. **Test the mapping:** Hold the pose fixed while changing velocities; check whether the numerical readout and arrows agree.
6. **Demo the viewer:** Play the humanoid motion with pause, scrub, and numeric readouts so another student can inspect a surprising frame.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Positions and velocities] --> D[CoM and momentum]
  S --> R[Render humanoid]
  D --> O[Labeled overlays]
  R --> O
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Mixed units:** Linear and angular momentum do not share units; a single unlabelled arrow scale makes them misleading.
- **False stability claims:** The CoM marker alone does not describe contacts, actuator limits, or whether a motion can actually execute.

## When it's done

- **Worked check:** With every generalized velocity zero, momentum must be zero even when the bent humanoid's CoM is not at the origin.
- **Repeatable delivery:** Save model revision, motion, vector conventions, and checks for stationary motion, an empty trajectory, and incompatible state dimensions.

```python
com = pin.centerOfMass(model, data, q, v)
momentum = pin.computeCentroidalMomentum(model, data, q, v)
print(com, momentum.linear, momentum.angular)
```

lessons.name: Click-to-reach SO-101
lessons.summary: Turn a camera-image click into a tabletop target for the SO-101, rejecting targets that cannot be reached safely.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Turn a camera-image click into a tabletop target for the SO-101, rejecting targets that cannot be reached safely.

![SO-101 follower arm used for the proposed camera-click reaching interface](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-click.webp)
*SO-101 follower arm used for the proposed camera-click reaching interface. Source: [Published setup](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/so101), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **An image click** supplies two pixel coordinates, not a full position in space; constrain the exercise to a calibrated tabletop plane rather than guessing depth.
- **Inverse kinematics (IK)** converts the resulting robot-frame target into joint angles; an acceptable position does not imply every gripper orientation is achievable.
- **The interface** resembles a web request pipeline: parse the click, validate coordinates, solve the request, and reject invalid outputs before causing side effects.

> **Key idea:** A click is a request for a checked motion, never permission to send arbitrary joint commands.

## What you need

- **Preparation:** Complete Assemble & teleoperate an SO-101 and Camera-to-gripper frame chain on the SO-101; keep the camera and table fixed.
- **Software:** Use OpenCV calibration, a documented SO-101 model, an IK solver, and a simulator; extra hardware cost depends on existing lab equipment.
- **A restricted task:** Start with reaching above marked tabletop points, not picking objects of unknown height; learn Inverse kinematics (analytic & numerical).

## Steps

1. **Calibrate the scene:** Estimate camera intrinsics, distortion, and table pose from known reference points; retain their physical scale.
2. **Map the click:** Undistort the pixel, form its viewing ray, and intersect that ray with the known table plane.
3. **Transform the target:** Express the intersection in robot-base coordinates and add a deliberately chosen approach clearance.
4. **Solve the reach:** Use position and a feasible orientation constraint; inspect solver success, joint limits, and forward-kinematics error.
5. **Preview before execution:** Check the interpolated path for collisions and limits in simulation, then require explicit confirmation for slow hardware motion.
6. **Demo the interface:** Mark accepted and rejected clicks differently and log target, resulting pose, and reason for each refusal.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Pixel click] --> R[Ray meets table]
  R --> B[Robot target]
  B --> I[IK solution]
  I --> V[Path validation]
  V --> A[Confirmed slow reach]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Depth ambiguity:** A pixel over a tall object does not identify its top surface when the interface assumes the tabletop.
- **Endpoint-only checking:** IK does not establish a collision-free route; the elbow can strike the table while the final gripper pose appears valid.
- **Hardware hazard:** Keep the arm's swept volume clear and a motor-power disconnect within reach during confirmed tests.

## When it's done

- **Worked round trip:** Project a known tabletop marker into the image, click its location, and compare the recovered base-frame point with the marker's measured position.
- **Visible failure handling:** Demonstrate normal clicks, unreachable clicks, a ray with no valid forward table intersection, and absent camera frames without moving on invalid input.

```text
Pseudocode with vectors expressed in the same frame:
if abs(dot(normal, ray_direction)) > epsilon:
    distance = dot(normal, plane_point - ray_origin) / dot(normal, ray_direction)
    if distance > 0:
        target = ray_origin + distance * ray_direction
```

lessons.name: Closed-loop leg linkage in MuJoCo
lessons.summary: Export a four-bar leg mechanism into MuJoCo, close its kinematic loop with constraints, and inspect its motion and closure error.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Export a four-bar leg mechanism into MuJoCo, close its kinematic loop with constraints, and inspect its motion and closure error.

![Rhoban's planar closed-chain reference shown cut open into a tree before closure constraints](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-linkage.webp)
*Rhoban's planar closed-chain reference shown cut open into a tree before closure constraints. Source: [Published setup](https://onshape-to-robot.readthedocs.io/en/latest/kinematic_loops.html), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **A four-bar linkage** is a loop of rigid links joined by pivots; for this exercise, use one fixed base and moving links that form a simple leg mechanism.
- **A kinematic tree** has one parent per body; closing a mechanical loop requires an additional relationship beyond that tree.
- **An equality constraint** asks the simulator to keep specified points or poses together. Think of a database integrity constraint connecting records stored in separate branches.

> **Key idea:** Cutting a loop makes the model representable as a tree; closure constraints restore the missing mechanical relationship.

## What you need

- **Software:** Use Onshape, authorized API access, onshape-to-robot, and MuJoCo; this project requires no physical leg or printed parts.
- **Preparation:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim and study Parallel & closed-chain mechanisms plus Robot description formats (URDF / MJCF).
- **Reference versus deliverable:** Rhoban's pictured planar mechanism explains loop handling; adapt that method to your own four-bar leg rather than calling the reference a four-bar.

## Steps

1. **Design the mechanism:** Define pivot locations, rigid links, and a fixed base; verify its intended movement in CAD before export.
2. **Choose the tree cut:** Add the closing mate with the closing_ prefix so the exporter can identify the missing relationship.
3. **Separate active and passive joints:** Drive the intended input; mark passive joints as not actuated rather than commanding every pivot independently.
4. **Export and inspect:** Select MuJoCo output and check the generated equality elements, joint axes, limits, and initial assembly.
5. **Sweep slowly:** Move through valid input positions while recording the distance between the two cut-side reference points.
6. **Demo the result:** Replay the moving leg beside its input angle and closure-error trace, including positions where motion must stop.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[CAD loop] --> T[Tree and closing mate]
  T --> E[Export equality constraints]
  E --> S[Input joint sweep]
  S --> P[Motion and closure plot]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Overconstraining:** Actuating passive joints can demand incompatible motions; a numerically jittering mechanism is not evidence of working leg control.
- **Incorrect closure type:** The exporter uses weld for fixed closure, connect for ball closure, and two connect constraints for revolute closure.
- **Ignoring residuals:** Visually overlapping parts can still have constraint error; measure the cut-side points instead of trusting the rendered meshes.

## When it's done

- **Worked configuration:** Set a fixed base with freejoint false and set actuated false for passive joints, matching the documented planar export example.
- **Reproducible package:** Save CAD revision, exported model, sweep inputs, and closure plots; report invalid initial geometry and failed sweeps rather than hiding them.

```json
{
  "output_format": "mujoco",
  "freejoint": false,
  "joint_properties": {"passive_joint": {"actuated": false}}
}
```
